prompt: I'm trying to decide between two job offers and I want to think this through carefully before I answer them. Please analyze the trade-offs step by step. Offer A is a senior backend role at a mid-size fintech company: $185k base salary, ten percent annual bonus, equity refreshed yearly, fully remote within the US, a team of about forty engineers, and an on-call rotation roughly once every six weeks. Offer B is a staff engineer role at an early-stage climate startup that just closed its series B, sixty people total: $165k base, meaningful but illiquid equity, hybrid three days a week in Chicago, no formal on-call process yet but that will certainly change as they grow, and the technical scope is much broader — I would own the ingestion pipeline, the deployment story, and probably hiring two more engineers within a year. I care most about long-term financial outcome and interesting technical problems, less about prestige, and I have about eight years of experience so I'm at the point where the title on my resume might matter for the next jump but shouldn't dominate. I'd also like you to evaluate which role is riskier if the economy turns bad in the next two years, because the startup obviously carries more of that risk than the fintech, and compare the realistic five-year financial outcomes including equity under pessimistic and optimistic scenarios for the startup's valuation. Explain why you land where you do rather than just giving me a verdict.
because: Long (well over 600 chars) deep-reasoning request with explicit keywords; the long_complex_prompt rule fires correctly today.

prompt: I've been going back and forth on whether to refinance my mortgage and I want help thinking it all the way through rather than a quick answer. Here's the situation. I bought my house three years ago at a 6.75 percent rate on a thirty-year fixed mortgage with about $310,000 still owed. Rates have come down and I can get quoted 5.5 percent today with roughly $4,100 in closing costs, some of which the lender says it can roll into the loan. My monthly payment right now is about $2,015 and the new one would be around $1,760 on a fresh thirty-year term. I plan to stay in the house for at least another seven years but probably not more than twelve, since the kids will be out of school by then and we've talked about moving somewhere smaller. I have about $40,000 in a savings account earning 4 percent, no other debt besides a car loan with two years left at 3.9 percent, and I'm currently maxing out my 401k match but not contributing beyond it. What I can't get my head around is whether the breakeven math changes much if I pay the closing costs upfront versus rolling them in, and whether it makes more sense to take the lower rate on a fifteen-year term instead, which my bank says I'd qualify for at 5.25 but the payment would be close to what I pay now so there'd be no monthly relief, just interest savings. There's also the question of whether I should keep the cash cushion at all given the savings yield, or use part of it to buy down the rate by a quarter point, which the lender quotes at about $2,900. Please work through all of this with me, lay out the numbers under each of the scenarios I've described, tell me which option comes out ahead over both a seven-year and a twelve-year horizon, and be explicit about the assumptions you're making where I've left things vague.

prompt: Write a story about a lighthouse keeper on a remote rocky island who has worked the same light for thirty-one years and has never once seen a ship get close enough to need it. I want it to be a slow, atmospheric piece in the tradition of gothic coastal fiction, somewhere between three and four thousand words, told in close third person limited to the keeper's perspective, with the weather functioning almost as a second character. The keeper should be practical and unsentimental on the surface — someone who keeps immaculate logs and talks to the gulls only because it keeps his voice working — but the story should gradually reveal that he stayed all these years because of one night early in his posting when he fell asleep on watch during a storm and a fishing boat went onto the rocks anyway, and the village below never learned why the light was dark. Bring in a supply boat captain who visits monthly and slowly pieces the truth together over years of small conversations. End ambiguously: a modern container ship appears on a collision course in heavy fog, the keeper climbs the tower, and the last paragraph should leave genuinely unresolved whether the light he tends this time actually matters or whether he simply needs it to. Avoid melodrama, keep the prose restrained, and use the log-book entries as a recurring structural device between sections.
because: Long-form creative brief over 500 chars with an explicit 'write a story' keyword; the rule fires correctly today.
